Summary: Widdows and Peters (2003) asked whether logical connectives could be defined directly on distributional word vectors, so that the geometric flexibility of vector semantics is combined with the crispness of Boolean querying. They defined negation as orthogonal projection, where 'a NOT b' removes from a the component along b, and disjunction as the linear subspace spanned by several vectors. Extended negation, 'a NOT (b1 OR … OR bn)', projects a onto the orthogonal complement of that subspace. The authors showed that these operators coincide with the connectives of Birkhoff–von Neumann quantum logic. This was the first explicit use of quantum logic in natural language processing. The operators were tested on word vectors built from roughly 173 million words of New York Times text. Qualitative neighbour lists showed that negation removes unwanted senses of ambiguous words, for example the legal sense of 'suit' or the sporting sense of 'play'. The paper itself gives no quantitative retrieval scores and defers them to companion work. The approach is quantum-inspired: it borrows the lattice of subspaces and runs entirely on classical hardware. Its relevance for autonomous agents is that it supplies a projective, non-distributive semantics for concept negation and exclusion. This is the same projector algebra used by QP decision models.

Summary: Sordoni et al. (2013) proposed the Quantum Language Model (QLM) for ad hoc retrieval. The aim was to capture dependencies between query terms without the combinatorial blow-up of n-gram or Markov random field (MRF) models. In QLM, single terms and compound term dependencies are encoded as projectors in a Hilbert space whose dimension equals the vocabulary. A query or document is a density matrix, estimated by maximum likelihood from the sequence of projectors it contains. The density matrix is thus a generalised probability distribution over subspaces rather than over sets of terms. Documents are then ranked by a divergence between query and document density matrices, a quantum generalisation of the KL-divergence ranking of classical language models. The model was evaluated on standard TREC ad hoc collections and compared with bag-of-words and MRF-based dependency baselines. It was reported to be competitive with or better than these baselines. Numerical gains are not reproduced here because the full text was not read. The approach is quantum-inspired: it borrows the density-matrix formalism but runs on classical hardware. Its main limitation is the cost of estimating a vocabulary-sized density matrix. The paper matters because it introduced density matrices as learnable state representations, which later neural quantum-inspired models inherited.

Summary: Biamonte et al. (2017) is the widely cited Nature review of quantum machine learning. It surveys quantum algorithms for linear algebra, including HHL-type solvers, as well as quantum principal component analysis, support vector machines, Boltzmann machines, sampling and optimisation. It also examines the input/output bottlenecks that limit claimed speed-ups. This review cites it as the canonical reference for genuinely quantum-hardware machine learning. That field is distinct from the quantum-like and quantum-inspired models on classical computers that are the survey's main subject.

Summary: Schuld and Killoran (2019) interpret the encoding of classical inputs into a quantum state as a nonlinear feature map into a 'feature Hilbert space', making quantum computing formally analogous to kernel methods. They propose two classifiers. In one, a quantum device estimates an intractable kernel for a support vector machine. In the other, a variational circuit acts as a linear model. A squeezing feature map on two-dimensional toy data illustrates this. This review cites it as the foundational quantum-hardware kernel link.

Summary: Uprety et al. (2020) review quantum-theory-inspired information retrieval (QIR), work that since 2004 has used Hilbert-space representations and quantum probability in retrieval on classical hardware. The authors organise the field into two strands. The first is representation and ranking, covering density-matrix and complex-valued language models and quantum-inspired neural matching. The second is user interaction and cognition, covering order effects and interference in relevance judgements and incompatibility between judgement perspectives. They stress that QIR is distinct from quantum computing and lay out a road-map of open problems. The survey uses it as the reference map of QP-based retrieval and user modelling.

Summary: Widdows et al. (2021) is a tutorial-style review of the mathematics that quantum mechanics and artificial intelligence share. It covers vector spaces, scalar products, subspaces and implication, orthogonal projection and negation, dual vectors, density matrices, positive operators and tensor products. For each tool it gives applications in information retrieval, categorisation and hypernymy, word-sense modelling, knowledge-base inference, decision making and semantic composition. It also notes which methods might eventually run on quantum hardware. The survey uses it to explain why QP models of cognition and vector-based AI can share one formal toolkit, and to separate mathematical borrowing from claims about quantum hardware.

Summary: Berner et al. (2021) proposed a quantum algorithm for Bayesian neural network inference and prediction. It builds on quantum inner-product estimation from quantum deep learning. Because posterior sampling tolerates noise, a single quantum estimate per sample may suffice. In classical simulations on regression, binary classification and four UCI datasets, accuracy approached the classical results at about 10–13 qubits. This review cites it as a hardware-oriented example of combining quantum computation with Bayesian uncertainty. That is distinct from quantum-like cognition models.

Summary: Lorenz et al. (2023) ran compositional natural language processing (NLP) models on real quantum hardware. They exploited the formal correspondence between the DisCoCat model of meaning and quantum theory: a pregroup-grammar parse of a sentence is compiled into a parametrised quantum circuit. Word meanings are trainable circuit parameters, and the output qubit's measurement statistics give the class label. Quantum analogues of a bag-of-words model and a word-sequence model served as syntax-free and word-order-only baselines. There were two binary tasks. The first was meaning classification (MC), with 130 grammar-generated sentences about food or IT. The second was relative-pronoun (RP) classification, with 105 noun phrases from RelPron. Models were trained with SPSA in noiseless simulation and then on IBM's 5-qubit superconducting device ibmq_bogota. For DisCoCat, the simulated train and test errors after 500 iterations were 16.9% and 20.2% for MC, and 9.4% and 27.7% for RP. On hardware, the test errors were 16.7% for MC and 32.3% for RP, with F-scores of 0.85 and 0.75. As expected, syntax-sensitive DisCoCat did best on RP, while simpler models suited MC. The main limitations are the tiny datasets, a single hardware run per task, costly post-selection, and hardware queues of about 12 to 72 hours. The authors explicitly claim no quantum advantage. For autonomous agents, the work is a benchmark for what genuinely quantum language processing can do on current noisy hardware.

Summary: Nausheen et al. (2025) present a systematic literature review of quantum natural language processing (QNLP) covering 2012–2024, using explicit inclusion criteria. They classify models by quantum-computing principle, architecture and computational approach: categorical/DisCoCat, quantum probabilistic, quantum circuit, quantum kernel, quantum language models and hybrid quantum–classical models. They also cover encodings of classical text into quantum states and quantum optimisation for hyperparameter tuning. They count how often each method is used across NLP tasks. They conclude that QNLP remains limited to small datasets and a few well-explored models. This review cites it for this landscape and for its sober assessment of scale.

Summary: Svozil (2025) proposed an alternative to dynamic, transformer-based handling of polysemy. Each word is a single static unit vector in a Hilbert space, and linguistic contexts are maximal observables, that is, orthonormal bases. A word vector gets its specific meaning from the basis, or context, in which it is considered. Because in dimension three or higher one vector can belong to several mutually complementary bases, called intertwining contexts, 'run' can sit in separate contexts with 'exercise', 'business' or 'river'. The construction is illustrated with orthogonality hypergraphs and the twelve-element 'firefly' logic. The author also suggests building self-adjoint operators from contextual bases as a more compact encoding. The paper is a short conceptual note of about five pages. It has no learning algorithm, no corpus and no evaluation, and it leaves learning of the intertwined bases from data to future work. The idea is quantum-inspired and entirely classical. It matters for autonomous agents because it gives a Kochen–Specker-style account of context-dependent meaning. An agent's language or concept module could represent complementary interpretations without a separate vector for each sense.

Summary: Stoudenmire and Schwab (2016) adapted optimisation algorithms for tensor networks, developed in quantum many-body physics, to supervised learning. Each input is mapped by a local feature map into a product state, which is a tensor product of small vectors, one per pixel. The weight tensor of a linear classifier over this exponentially large space is then parameterised as a matrix product state (MPS), also known as a tensor train. Training uses a DMRG-like sweeping algorithm. It updates pairs of adjacent tensors and adapts the bond dimension, the rank of each bond, through singular value decomposition. On the MNIST handwritten-digit dataset the authors report a test-set classification error below 1%. They also discuss the extra structure the tensor-network form gives the model and suggest a possible generative interpretation. This is a quantum-inspired method in the strict sense: it uses the mathematics of quantum states, but everything runs on classical hardware, and no cognitive claim is made. Limitations include evaluation on a single, simple benchmark, and a fixed one-dimensional ordering of the input that ignores two-dimensional image structure. For autonomous agents and robots, it shows that Hilbert-space state representations can be compressed and trained efficiently at scale. This bears on the feasibility of quantum-like models in real agents.

Summary: Zhang et al. (2018) proposed a quantum many-body wave function inspired language model (QMWF-LM) for text matching. The resulting model thus gives a quantum-many-body reading of CNN-based matching. It was evaluated on question answering and answer selection benchmarks against classical neural and earlier quantum language model baselines, and was reported to be effective. Specific scores are not given here because the paper's full text was not read. The model is quantum-inspired and runs on classical hardware. The analogy constrains the architecture rather than implying any physical quantum process. Its limitations are that interpretability rests on the analogy and that the evaluation covers only text matching. For autonomous agents, the paper shows how tensor-product state spaces from QP cognition can be learned with standard deep-learning tools.

Summary: Li et al. (2019) introduced the Complex-valued Network for Matching (CNM), which applies quantum-probability mathematics to language modelling. Words are pure quantum states and sentences are mixed states, so each sentence is a density matrix. All of these are represented in a single complex-valued vector space. Each word embedding has an amplitude and a phase, and a sentence's density matrix is a weighted mixture of its word states. Matching between a question and a candidate answer is computed through trainable quantum measurements, that is, projections onto learned measurement vectors. The network's components are constrained so that each has an explicit physical meaning, which the authors present as a route to interpretability. On two standard question-answering benchmarks, CNM performed comparably to strong CNN and RNN baselines. The abstract gives no numbers, and none are quoted here. The paper won the NAACL 2019 best explainable NLP paper award. The model is quantum-inspired: it borrows the density-matrix and measurement formalism but runs entirely on classical hardware. Limitations are that performance is comparable to, not better than, baselines, and that the interpretability claims are not tested with users. For autonomous agents, CNM shows that learned density-matrix states and projective measurements can serve as an interpretable decision layer.

Summary: Li et al. (2021) addressed multimodal fusion for video sentiment analysis with a quantum-inspired framework. It was evaluated on standard multimodal video sentiment benchmarks and compared with state-of-the-art fusion networks. The authors report competitive effectiveness together with greater transparency about how modalities combine. Specific benchmark scores are not given because the full text was not read. The model is quantum-inspired rather than quantum-like: it does not fit human judgement data, and 'entanglement' refers to a mathematical structure, not a physical resource. Its limitations are that it is specific to sentiment tasks and that interpretability is argued rather than measured. The network's weights are learned with an existing algorithm for training such complex-valued quantum-inspired layers, so the model can be trained in a data-driven, end-to-end way. The authors evaluated it on two standard conversational emotion-recognition benchmarks. The authors also argue that it offers a quantum view for understanding conversational emotion recognition. The model is quantum-inspired and runs on classical hardware. Summary: Gkoumas et al. (2021) treated video sentiment analysis as a decision-fusion problem subject to cognitive-bias-like effects. Following quantum cognition, they hypothesised that the sentiment judgements from different modalities may be incompatible: their order matters, and they cannot be measured jointly for a single decision. Each utterance is represented as a superposition state in a complex-valued Hilbert space. The unimodal classifiers, for text, vision and audio, are modelled as incompatible observables and implemented as positive-operator-valued measures (POVMs). Fusion then follows the QP rules for sequential and incompatible measurements rather than classical averaging or voting. The model was evaluated on two video sentiment benchmarks against both decision-level and content-level fusion methods. According to the abstract, it substantially outperformed these baselines. It also handled every combination pattern of unimodal predictions, including the extreme case where all unimodal classifiers are wrong. Numerical margins are not quoted here. The approach is quantum-like in structure, since it uses the QP rules of cognition, but it is fitted to annotated benchmark labels, not to human decision data, and it runs on classical hardware. A limitation is that the incompatibility is assumed rather than tested. For autonomous agents, it is a direct template for QP-based fusion of conflicting sensor-level decisions.

Summary: Cerezo et al. (2021) proved that barren plateaus, or exponentially vanishing gradients, depend on the cost function in variational quantum algorithms. With global observables, gradients vanish exponentially even for shallow alternating layered circuits. With local observables and depth O(log n), gradients vanish at worst polynomially. Simulations with up to 100 qubits of a quantum autoencoder illustrate the result. This review cites it as a key trainability constraint on genuinely quantum-hardware learning agents.

Summary: Binz and Schulz (2023) applied cognitive-psychology paradigms to GPT-3, using both vignette-based problems and task-based experiments on decision making, information search, deliberation and causal reasoning. Summary: Uprety et al. (2024) asked whether large language models (LLMs) reproduce the order effects that humans show in similarity judgements. The motivation is alignment: LLM-based agents increasingly make decisions and take actions in real-world settings, and human judgements are themselves affected by cognitive biases. The authors replicated a well-known human study showing order effects in similarity judgements, in which the rated similarity of two items depends on which is presented first. They administered the same judgements to several popular LLMs under different prompt settings. They report the specific settings in which LLMs show human-like order-effect bias and those in which they do not. They then discuss what these findings imply for designing LLM-based applications. The work is framed as an ongoing investigation. The abstract does not give the list of models, the sampling settings or quantitative effect sizes, so none are given here. The study comes from the quantum cognition and information retrieval group, and order effects are the standard QP signature of incompatible judgements. The paper, however, probes the effect empirically rather than fitting a QP model. Its limitations are its preliminary scope and its dependence on prompts. For autonomous agents, it shows that order-dependent judgement can surface in LLM decision components and should be audited.

Summary: Maksimovic and Maksymov (2025) looked at image-classification systems that fail with confusing or erroneous outputs, or that defer difficult cases to human operators. They asked whether a quantum-cognition-motivated network could emulate human-like perception, confidence and uncertainty. They used the recently proposed quantum-tunnelling neural network (QT-NN), whose activation function is inspired by the quantum-mechanical probability of a particle tunnelling through a potential barrier. Its outputs are interpreted in the light of quantum cognition theory as human-like judgements. The network was trained to classify image datasets, and its confidence and uncertainty patterns were compared with those expected in human decision making. The authors report that the QT-NN provides evidence of human-like decision-making. It could also be trained up to 50 times faster than a classical counterpart. These claims come from the abstract, and the datasets and the comparison protocol were not checked here. The model is quantum-inspired: it runs on classical hardware and uses a physics-derived activation rather than QP state updating. A limitation is that human-likeness is judged against simulated human decisions rather than behavioural data from participants. For human–AI teaming, the work points to classifiers whose uncertainty is closer to human uncertainty and therefore easier for operators to interpret.

Summary: Lo et al. (2025) gave the first large-scale test of quantum-like contextuality in natural language. They used a large language model as the source of probability distributions. The authors built a linguistic schema, 'PR-anaphora', modelled on the minimal contextual measurement scenario, the 3-cyclic scenario, whose strongly contextual model is PR-box-like. Each instance has two nouns, three adjectives and two pronouns, framed as a co-reference resolution problem. Noun pairs sharing adjectives were extracted from Simple English Wikipedia, giving 866,108 noun pairs and 51,966,480 instances. Empirical models were then built from bert-base-uncased predictions. Contextuality was assessed with two frameworks that tolerate signalling: a signalling-corrected sheaf-theoretic criterion and Contextuality-by-Default (CbD). Of all instances, 77,118 (0.148%) were sheaf-contextual and 36,938,948 (71.1%) were CbD-contextual. The authors derived a relation between the degree of contextuality and the Euclidean distance between BERT embedding vectors. Regression identified this distance as the best predictor of contextuality. Restricting the data to the top 1% most similar noun pairs raised the rates to 0.50% (sheaf) and 81.83% (CbD). The analysis is quantum-like and runs on classical hardware. Limitations are that it uses a single masked language model and a synthetic schema, and that it does not show that contextuality improves any task. For autonomous agents, it provides tools for detecting contextuality in the belief states of language-model components.

Summary: Aerts et al. (2026) asked whether the non-classical probability structures previously found in human conceptual combination also appear when large language models (LLMs) act as the 'participants'. They carried out two tests. In the first, ChatGPT and Google Gemini judged conceptual combinations within a Bell-type design. The abstract reports that Bell's inequalities were significantly violated, which indicates a probability model that does not satisfy Kolmogorov's axioms. In the second test, the same models generated text, and word distributions in large texts followed Bose–Einstein rather than Maxwell–Boltzmann statistics. Both results mirror the authors' earlier findings from human participants and corpus analyses. The authors interpret this as evidence of convergence between human and artificial cognition, driven by a meaning-bearing structure in semantic vector spaces rather than by network architecture. The analysis is quantum-like: QP structure is detected in LLM outputs on classical hardware. The CHSH values and sample sizes are in the full text, which was not read, so they are not reported here. Limitations include the dependence of LLM outputs on prompts and model versions, uncontrolled signalling in Bell tests, and the interpretive step from statistical signature to shared cognitive structure. For AI systems, the paper suggests that QP structure may emerge from language training without being built in.

Summary: Imannezhad et al. (2026) compared GPT-5's probability judgements with those of humans on a task known to elicit classical-probability violations. The violations considered were conjunction fallacies, disjunction fallacies and breaches of binary complementarity. The authors used an existing large human dataset, in which participants showed several types of fallacy, and ran GPT-5 on the same task. Each session was matched to a participant's profile, giving 553 persona sessions. Unlike the humans, GPT-5 produced only single conjunction or disjunction fallacies. It also complied almost perfectly with binary complementarity. The article reports conjunction-fallacy rates of about 18.8% for GPT-5 against 58.5% for humans, and double conjunction fallacies of 0.5% against 37.0%. The model's overall pattern matched the predictions of early quantum-probability models of judgement better than later variants that add noise. The authors conclude that GPT-5 reasons about probability more coherently and consistently than naïve human participants. The study is quantum-like: QP models are used as the theoretical yardstick for both humans and the LLM. Limitations are that only one proprietary model was tested and that personas are an imperfect proxy for real participants. For human–AI teaming, the study shows that LLM advisers cannot be assumed to share human biases, which matters when an AI system models or supports human decisions.

Summary: Kang (2026) turned the QQ equality into an audit criterion for sequential yes/no judgements by autoregressive large language models (LLMs). The QQ equality is a parameter-free prediction of the projective quantum question-order model, which human survey data approximately satisfy. On the theoretical side, the author characterised the mechanism families that satisfy QQ robustly. Summary: Dong et al. (2008) propose quantum reinforcement learning (QRL), which recasts the states and actions of a reinforcement-learning problem as eigenstates and eigenactions of a quantum system. The state–action space is represented as a superposition; an action is selected by a simulated measurement that collapses the action superposition, with probabilities given by squared amplitudes, and rewards update the amplitudes through a Grover-type amplitude-amplification step, so that exploration and exploitation are balanced by the amplitudes rather than by an ε-greedy or softmax rule. The authors analyse convergence and optimality and argue that, on genuine quantum hardware, quantum parallelism could update many state values at once. The simulated experiments, run on a classical computer in a gridworld navigation task, compare QRL with TD(0) using ε-greedy exploration; the preprint reports that QRL learns faster and converges over a much wider range of learning rates. The limitations are that the 'quantum' algorithm is only simulated classically, the environments are small tabular problems, and no physical implementation or function approximation is provided. The paper founded the Dong–Chen line of quantum and quantum-inspired RL (Dong et al. (2012), Wei et al. (2022)) and is a common reference point for quantum decision rules in autonomous agents.

Summary: Dong et al. (2012) address the sensitivity of reinforcement learning (RL) to learning rates and initial settings in mobile-robot navigation. They propose a quantum-inspired RL (QiRL) algorithm in which each state carries a superposition-like vector of action amplitudes: action selection is probabilistic, mimicking measurement collapse, and reinforcement adjusts amplitudes by a rule inspired by Grover-type amplitude amplification; a convergence result is stated for the temporal-difference value update. Everything runs on classical hardware. The method is first tested on a 58-state Markovian transition task, where QiRL converged after about 2000 episodes from four different start states, whereas a TD baseline needed between 1000 and 4000 episodes depending on the start state, and QiRL performed well for learning rates from 0.01 to 0.12 while TD failed to converge for rates of 0.02 and above. It is then evaluated in a simulated 600 × 400 grid world with 16 range sensors (obstacle avoidance) and on a real two-wheeled robot, MT-R, which learned to follow an office corridor into a target room. Limitations are the tabular state representation, comparison against a single TD baseline, and a largely qualitative real-robot demonstration. The work is an early example of quantum-inspired exploration rules transferred to physical robot learning.

Summary: Briegel and De las Cuevas (2012) propose projective simulation (PS), a model of a learning agent that, before acting, 'projects itself' into possible future situations by running a random walk through a network of clips, i.e. elementary patches of episodic memory. This episodic and compositional memory is updated by adapting transition probabilities between clips on reward, by adding clips from new percepts, and by composing new clips from existing ones, which the authors present as an elementary form of creative behaviour. Emotion tags on transitions record remembered rewards and allow a 'reflection' mechanism in which the agent repeats its internal simulation when the proposed action is not tagged as rewarded. The model is illustrated with a simulated invasion game, in which a defender agent learns to block an attacker from symbolic cues; learning curves show that a forgetting (dissipation) parameter trades adaptation speed against maximum blocking efficiency, and that a longer reflection time speeds up learning. The simulations are small and classical, and no comparison with standard RL benchmarks is made. The paper matters for the survey because the random walk over clips is designed to generalise naturally to quantum walks, providing the basis for later quantum-enhanced agents (Paparo et al. (2014)).

Summary: Paparo et al. (2014) ask whether quantum physics can speed up the internal deliberation of an autonomous learning agent, a bottleneck when the environment allows only limited time to respond. They consider the reflecting projective simulation (PS) agent of Briegel and De las Cuevas (2012), whose deliberation amounts to mixing a Markov chain over its episodic-memory clip network and checking whether the sampled clip is a flagged (rewarded) action. Replacing the classical random walk with a Szegedy-type quantum walk, combined with Grover-like reflections over flagged actions, they construct a quantum agent that outputs actions from approximately the same distribution as the classical agent. They prove that the number of calls to the diffusion operators scales as Õ(1/√(εδ)), where ε is the probability of flagged actions and δ the spectral gap, a quadratic improvement over the classical agent. The result is purely theoretical: it assumes a classical task environment, reversible Markov chains (with extension claimed for irreducible chains), and quantum memory that could be implemented with linear optics or trapped ions, none of which is demonstrated. For autonomous agents it provides the clearest formal case that genuine quantum hardware can accelerate an agent's decision time rather than just its offline learning.

Summary: Melnikov et al. (2018) benchmark the projective simulation (PS) agent of Briegel and De las Cuevas (2012) against standard tabular reinforcement learning. They apply PS, Q-learning and SARSA to two classic navigation problems, a grid world and the mountain car task, and compare learning performance and the effort needed to tune model parameters. According to the abstract, PS and the standard methods perform qualitatively and quantitatively similarly, but optimal PS parameters are much easier to find, with computational effort for parameter selection reduced by one to two orders of magnitude, because PS has few model parameters. The study is entirely classical and uses small tabular benchmarks, so it says nothing directly about quantum speed-up; its value is in showing that the classical PS model, which admits a quantum-walk generalisation (Paparo et al. (2014)), is a competitive baseline learner. For the survey, it anchors claims about PS-based agents in robotics to a standard benchmark comparison rather than to toy games such as the invasion game alone.

(2020) provide a formal convergence analysis of projective simulation (PS), the episodic-memory learning model of Briegel and De las Cuevas (2012) that admits quantum speed-ups in deliberation. This review cites it as the theoretical guarantee that PS-based agents, including those proposed for robots, are sound reinforcement learners and not merely heuristics.

Summary: Flamini et al. (2020) present a blueprint for a photonic learning machine that implements reinforcement-learning algorithms (SARSA, Q-learning and projective simulation) through single-photon evolution on a mesh of tunable beam splitters. Numerical studies in standard RL environments show that realistic experimental noise can be tolerated or even helpful. This review cites it as a concrete near-term hardware route for quantum-compatible learning agents.

Summary: Chen et al. (2020) investigate whether variational quantum circuits (VQCs) suitable for noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices can replace the neural network in deep Q-learning. They recast experience replay and the target network in a hybrid scheme where a VQC with computational-basis encoding approximates the Q-function, qubit expectation values give action values, and a classical optimiser trains the circuit parameters. The agents are tested on a 4×4 Frozen Lake grid (three configurations) and a cognitive-radio channel-selection task, simulated with PennyLane and with Qiskit Aer using noise models from an IBM Q 20-qubit machine; trained models were also run for five episodes on the IBM Q device ibmq-valencia. In Frozen Lake the circuit needs 28 parameters against 64 table entries for tabular Q-learning (a 56.25% reduction), and in the cognitive-radio task the authors report scores close to 100 in under ten iterations even with noise, converging faster than a single-hidden-layer network from prior work. The environments are very small, the classical comparison is indirect (taken from other papers' figures), and hardware runs are limited to inference. For autonomous agents this is an early proof of principle that genuinely quantum circuits can serve as RL function approximators, not evidence of practical advantage.

Summary: Saggio et al. (2021) report an experiment in which a reinforcement-learning agent learns faster because it interacts with its environment through a quantum communication channel, combined with classical communication to evaluate and control the improvement. The protocol runs on an integrated nanophotonic processor with telecom-wavelength photons and fast active feedback. This review cites it as the first experimental demonstration of reduced learning time for a quantum-enhanced agent, contrasting with purely theoretical speed-ups.

Summary: Jerbi et al. (2021) address two open problems for quantum reinforcement learning: no parametrised quantum circuit (PQC) policy had solved standard benchmarks, and no learning advantage over classical agents had been proven. They define RAW-PQC policies (action probabilities from Born-rule measurements) and SOFTMAX-PQC policies (a softmax over expectation values of trainable weighted observables), use data re-uploading with trainable input scaling, and train them with REINFORCE-style policy gradients, deriving how gradients can be estimated on a quantum device. In classically simulated experiments on CartPole-v1, MountainCar-v0 and Acrobot-v1 (2 to 6 qubits; 20 agents per learning curve), SOFTMAX-PQC agents learn substantially better than RAW-PQC agents and reach performance comparable to standard deep neural networks. They also construct PQC-generated environments on which DNN policies (best of depths 2–10, widths 8–64) perform poorly while SOFTMAX-PQC agents learn close-to-optimal policies, and prove a separation between PQC agents and any classical learner in environments built on the discrete logarithm problem. The limitations are that benchmark gains are not advantages, the separating tasks are artificial, and no hardware is used. The paper is a key reference for the claim that quantum policies may, in principle, offer agents capabilities classical learners lack.

Summary: Wei et al. (2022) propose deep reinforcement learning with quantum-inspired experience replay (DRL-QER), a classical training scheme that changes how transitions are sampled from the replay buffer. Each stored transition is given a quantum-like representation, a qubit-style amplitude, which is modified by a 'preparation' operation, relating its temporal-difference error to its importance in a manner inspired by amplitude amplification, and by a 'depreciation' operation that lowers the priority of transitions already replayed many times to preserve diversity. Sampling probabilities follow from these amplitudes, so the method adaptively balances exploration and exploitation in the choice of experiences. The authors evaluate DRL-QER on Atari 2600 games against prioritised experience replay (DRL-PER) and DCRL, and report in the abstract that it outperforms these methods on most games with improved training efficiency, and that it can be combined with double and dueling network architectures. No quantum hardware is involved; the 'quantum' element is a sampling heuristic whose advantage depends on tuning and has been shown mainly on game benchmarks. For autonomous agents it is a practical example of quantum-inspired ideas improving the sample efficiency of deep RL, continuing the line of Dong et al. (2008).

Summary: Skolik et al. (2022) study whether parametrised quantum circuits (PQCs) can serve as Q-function approximators in deep Q-learning and which architectural choices matter. Their hybrid agent uses data re-uploading, trainable input weights and, crucially, trainable output weights on the observables, because a PQC's output range is bounded by its measurement operators while optimal Q-values may be large. Ablation studies are run on Frozen Lake v0 and Cart Pole v0 in classical simulation, followed by an extensive hyperparameter search over PQCs and two-layer neural networks. On Cart Pole, neither re-uploading nor input weights alone solved the task within 5000 episodes, while combining them did (at most 3000 and 600 episodes on average for two hyperparameter sets). The best average PQC (25 layers, 302 parameters) solved Cart Pole in about 500 episodes, versus about 250 for the best network (562 parameters); the best individual PQC (62 parameters) needed 206 episodes against 186 for a 1142-parameter network. The authors also extend a known quantum–classical separation to Q-value inference in restricted environments. Limitations include simulation only, tiny tasks and training instability as PQC size grows. For robot and agent learning, the paper clarifies that readout design, not qubit count, determines whether quantum Q-learners work at all.

Summary: Acuto and Barill`a (2022) ask whether variational quantum circuits (VQCs) can reduce the model size of Soft Actor-Critic (SAC), a standard deep RL method for continuous robot control. They build a custom Box2D environment of a planar two-link robotic arm that must bring its end effector to a randomly placed target within 250 steps, and compare classical SAC with three hybrid variants: a VQC-based actor, VQC-based critics, and a full quantum SAC. Circuits use angle encoding with data re-uploading, are wrapped by classical layers and are simulated noiselessly in TensorFlow Quantum and Cirq. A hybrid actor (100 parameters) learned no better than a classical actor of similar size, and shrinking the classical critics prevented convergence, identifying the critic as the bottleneck. With hybrid critics (2600 parameters) the agent matched the classical learning curve with more than six times fewer parameters; the full quantum SAC (2700 parameters) converged, whereas a classical SAC with 3000 parameters did not and one with about 274k parameters did. Limitations are that all circuits are simulated without noise, the arm is a simple planar simulation, and parameter count is the only claimed advantage. For robotics, the paper illustrates the parameter-efficiency argument for quantum critics, not an advantage in wall-clock learning.

Summary: Sinha et al. (2025) propose Nav-Q, a quantum-supported deep RL method for collision-free navigation of self-driving cars that uses quantum computation only during training, so no quantum hardware is needed on board. Nav-Q is an advantage actor-critic agent (based on a classical NavA2C baseline with feature encoder and LSTM) in which the critic is a parametrised quantum circuit, while the actor that drives at test time remains classical. It is trained and tested on the CARLA-CTS 1.0 benchmark of pedestrian-related critical traffic scenarios in the CARLA simulator, with circuits simulated in PennyLane. The chosen 4-qubit, 2-layer critic converged faster than NavA2C in the first 4000 of 10,000 episodes; over six initialisations Nav-Q had a higher mean area under the return curve (2440.6 vs 2362.95) and lower standard deviation (758.78 vs 902.73). Driving policies were similar: Nav-Q reached goals slightly faster, the classical agent had slightly fewer crashes and near-misses, and the safety index was equal. Training took about 7–18 days per configuration, and simulated gate and depolarising noise degraded training while increasing exploration. The work is a realistic autonomous-driving testbed for quantum RL, but it shows stability gains rather than better driving.

Summary: Flamini et al. (2024) quantise projective simulation, an interpretable reinforcement-learning model whose decisions are random walks on a memory graph, using quantum walks of single photons in a lattice of tunable Mach–Zehnder interferometers trained with variational algorithms. In a transfer-learning example, the quantised agent exploits interference to gain capabilities beyond its classical counterpart. This review cites it for its argument that interference can be traced, supporting interpretable quantum learning agents.

Summary: Hohenfeld et al. (2024) test whether hybrid quantum deep RL, so far studied mostly on OpenAI Gym toys, scales to robot navigation. Parametrised quantum circuits with two encoding schemes (each state component on a separate qubit, or the whole state encoded consecutively on every qubit) serve as Q-function approximators in double deep Q-learning, with trainable output scaling, and are compared with classical neural-network baselines. The platform is a simulated Turtlebot 2 in three static grid-like environments (3×3, 4×4, 5×5, requiring roughly 20–45 steps) and a larger dynamic environment with lidar and moving obstacles; circuits are run in a noise-free simulator. Both quantum architectures solved all static tasks and, parameter for parameter, outperformed the networks: the best circuits had 444 and 480 parameters and matched networks about ten times larger in training steps, and with 300 parameters the circuits still solved the 5×5 task where equally small networks mostly failed. The classical baselines, however, trained faster and more stably, and outperformed both quantum models in the dynamic environment. The authors note their largest circuits have almost 200 gates per qubit and would not be viable on current hardware. This is a sober benchmark for quantum RL on robot tasks, showing parameter efficiency without practical advantage.

Summary: Lukac and Perkowski (2007) present an emotional model for Cynthea, a humanoid robot developed at Portland State University, organised in two levels. A cognitive level perceives the environment and executes behaviour scripts written in a robot command language, while an emotional level alters how those commands are executed, independently of their content, through string-rewriting operations such as repeating, modifying or deleting commands. The emotional level is modelled with quantum finite automata built from Hadamard and CNOT gates, over six emotional variables (anger, happiness, melancholy, depression, fear and contentment), so that superposition and entanglement generate less predictable, more lifelike behaviour; the quantum part runs on a software simulator, and dialogue relies on an existing chatbot system. As far as could be determined from the available text, no quantitative evaluation is reported and the authors describe the testing as partial. The quantum model is therefore a design proposal, and its behavioural benefit over a classical stochastic automaton is not demonstrated. The paper is nevertheless one of the earliest attempts to use quantum formalism, rather than quantum hardware, to drive robot affect, anticipating later quantum emotion models for robots (Yan et al. (2019)).

Summary: Aerts et al. (2011) is a short position paper that reviews the Brussels 'quantum interaction' programme and draws out its implications for artificial intelligence and robotics. The authors summarise how Hilbert-space and quantum-probability models, building on the SCoP (state–context–property) formalism, reproduce Hampton's membership-weight data on the conjunction and disjunction of concepts, including the Guppy (Pet-Fish) effect, and how related models address the disjunction effect and the Ellsberg paradox. From this they propose that human thought has two superposed layers: a classical logical layer and a non-Kolmogorovian quantum conceptual layer. For AI, they argue that tensor-product representations, as in Smolensky's binding proposal, could supply the word order and syntax that bag-of-words latent semantic analysis lacks. For robotics, they contrast the quantum-robot programme of Benioff (1998) and Dong et al. (2006), which relies on building real quantum computers, with the view that macroscopic, classically realised systems can carry quantum structure; they suggest that AI's shortfalls may stem from its reliance on classical computation. No new model, data or experiment is presented, and the claims about robotics remain speculative. The paper is nonetheless an early explicit statement of the idea that quantum-like cognition, rather than quantum hardware, could shape robot design.

Summary: Hangl et al. (2016) tackle generalisation in complex manipulation, such as bimanual or in-hand tasks, without large supervised datasets or complex controllers. Their idea is to keep simple controllers that work in a few specific situations and to have the robot 'play' with objects, using previously trained basis skills to estimate the state of the environment or to transform a novel situation into one where the solution is known; skills are organised hierarchically. Projective simulation (Briegel and De las Cuevas (2012)) serves as the learning mechanism, both for choosing which haptic sensing action to use and for choosing the preparatory skill given the perceived state. The approach is evaluated on a dual-arm robot in pick-and-place scenarios, notably grasping a book that may lie in different orientations and placing objects into a closed box, where the robot learned to use a flipping skill to open the lid. The authors report that sensing by sliding was far more reliable than poking or pressing, and roughly 80 roll-outs sufficed to reach 90% success in simulation based on real success rates. The state and skill sets are small and hand-designed and the learning is classical. It is an early demonstration of a quantum-compatible learning model (projective simulation) controlling a physical robot, later extended in Hangl et al. (2020).

Summary: Yan et al. (2019) propose a quantum emotion space (QES) for representing and manipulating a robot's emotional state. Building on a pleasure–arousal style model extended with time, emotions are encoded as sequences of entangled qubits, so that an emotional trajectory appears as a curve inside a cuboid, and transitions between emotions are expressed as unitary transformation matrices. The authors argue that this encoding needs fewer resources than a classical representation and makes it easy to track and manipulate emotional transitions over time, for instance with an 'emotion sensor'; as a proof of concept they show an inverse operation, implemented with quantum NOT gates, that maps an 'anger' state to a 'relaxation' state. The motivation is anticipatory: quantum robots, alone or in hybrid systems, may eventually need native emotional representations for human–robot interaction. The work is purely formal. According to the abstract and available summary there are no simulations on a robot, no human participants and no comparison with classical affect models, and the claimed resource savings would only materialise on quantum hardware. It is cited as the starting point of a quantum-computing approach to robot emotion (Yan et al. (2021), Yan et al. (2021)), distinct from quantum-probability models of human affect.

Summary: Moreira et al. (2020) is an open peer commentary on Lieder and Griffiths' target article proposing resource-rational analysis, which explains cognitive biases as optimal use of limited computational resources. The authors argue for an alternative, unifying framework based on quantum probability that yields more general cognitive and decision models able to represent more information than classical ones. They outline the ingredients of such a quantum-like cognitive architecture: indefinite (superposed) belief states represented as vectors in a Hilbert space, beliefs expressed through rotated bases, contextuality in the sense that no single joint distribution covers all decision contexts, and interference effects that account for violations of classical probability such as the disjunction effect. The commentary refers to their earlier quantum-like Bayesian network work (Moreira and Wichert (2016)) and to literature on contextuality in human judgement. It presents no new model, data or evaluation, and its argument that quantum models are more economical than resource-rational ones is asserted rather than demonstrated. For autonomous agents it is useful as a short, citable statement of what a quantum-like decision architecture would comprise, and of how it positions itself relative to bounded and resource-rational accounts that dominate classical agent design.

Summary: Lanza et al. (2020) explore whether quantum-probability formalisms, specifically state superposition and interference, can model robot perception in the way quantum cognition models human bistable perception such as binocular rivalry. In a deliberately minimal case study, a stationary circular robot with a front and a back presence sensor observes a randomly moving object. The relative frequency of back-sensor events within a time window is encoded into a single qubit by a Y-axis rotation, so that the qubit state summarises the robot's two mutually exclusive percepts and repeated measurements recover their probabilities. The model was run both as a classical simulation of the circuit and on real quantum processors of the IBM Quantum Experience: the designed behaviour was reproduced in simulation, whereas actual quantum hardware showed notable errors, particularly for unbalanced probability distributions. The authors therefore recommend simulation-based, quantum-like implementations over current quantum backends. The study is a feasibility check with binary percepts, a single object and no comparison with classical probabilistic perception, so it does not show any benefit of the quantum-like representation. It is nonetheless one of the first explicit transfers of quantum cognition to robot perception and motivates the multisensory extension in Lanza et al. (2021).

Summary: Hangl et al. (2020) address how a robot can extend manipulation skills that initially work only in a narrow range of situations. The robot plays autonomously with objects, applying previously trained skills and behaviours to learn how to bring a situation into one for which a successful strategy is already known. Behaviour selection uses projective simulation (Briegel and De las Cuevas (2012)), a classical reinforcement-learning model based on random walks through an episodic and compositional memory; the experience collected during play also trains an environment model that is used for active learning and for composing novel preparatory behaviours. The approach is demonstrated on a real dual-arm robot across several manipulation tasks, including book grasping, grasping objects of different sizes by selecting grasp strategies, placement on shelves and tower disassembly; composition allows previously unsolvable tasks such as tower disassembly to be solved. Using success statistics from the real-world trials, simulations indicate that active learning improves learning speed by around 30%. The method remains classical, relies on hand-designed skill libraries, supervision for rewards and a fixed sense–prepare–execute structure, and its scalability to large state spaces is untested. It is the clearest example in the corpus of a quantum-compatible learning model running on a physical robot.

Summary: Lanza et al. (2021) generalise their single-qubit quantum-like perception model (Lanza et al. (2020)) to integrate several sensory inputs into a multidimensional representation of the world. Each of n normalised sensor readings is encoded into its own qubit by a Y-rotation, so the joint register holds a superposition over 2^n basis states whose measurement probabilities express the robot's confidence in each world configuration; 'query operators' are defined that re-assign the meaning of basis states so that the robot's degree of belief in a particular target state can be read out. The demonstration uses a camera-like sensor whose average RGB values are treated as three scalar sensors, giving a three-qubit model simulated in IBM Qiskit; the model was evaluated over a systematic sampling of the colour space with 10^6 simulated measurements per input, showing a definite but non-linear relation between encoded inputs and measurement outcomes. There is no physical robot, no temporal integration in this version, each query destroys the state, and no comparison with classical Bayesian or fuzzy sensor fusion is made. The contribution is conceptual and formal: it shows how quantum-like state representations and projective queries could express graded belief in robot perception, but not that they improve it.

Summary: Yan et al. (2021) review artificial emotional intelligence for social robots, that is, methods that allow robots to recognise and express emotions in human–robot interaction. The review covers three areas: emotion classification, emotional robots, and emotion space modelling, including the authors' own quantum-computing-based emotion spaces and related work on the 'communication atmosphere' of multi-party interaction. It is intended as a compact compendium of progress in the field rather than a systematic review. This review cites it as the broader context for quantum emotion representations in robots (Yan et al. (2019), Yan et al. (2021)), showing how quantum encodings sit alongside classical dimensional emotion models, and as a pointer to the classical affective-computing baselines against which such proposals should be judged.

Summary: Yan et al. (2021) extend the quantum emotion space work of Yan et al. (2019) to companion robots by building on Plutchik's wheel of emotions, which arranges eight primary emotions with graded intensities. The authors define a quantum counterpart of the wheel model, in which emotional states are encoded in qubit registers arranged as a sequence of 'discs' forming an emotion space, and design quantum circuit schemes for generating an emotion and for transitions between emotions, so that changes of emotional state are realised as sequences of quantum gates. The motivation is that a quantum encoding can represent mixed and graded emotions compactly and may later run on quantum processors embedded in or connected to robots. We could not access the abstract or full text of this paper, only its title and figure captions, so the evaluation setting (simulation or hardware), any quantitative results and the exact circuit designs could not be verified. Like the earlier quantum emotion space, the approach appears to be a formal design without user studies or comparison with classical affect models. It is relevant to the survey as part of the quantum-computing strand of robot affect, which differs from quantum-probability models of human emotion and decision.

Summary: Ho and Hoorn (2022) attempt a quantum-computational construction of robot affect intended to handle ambiguous emotional states, probabilistic decisions and parallel cognitive processes in human–robot interaction. Their Quantum Coppélia (Q-Coppélia) translates the fuzzy-logic Silicon Coppélia model, which simulates how a robot's attitude towards its user develops, into quantum logic. Psychological scales are represented as qubits, so that superposition captures indefinite affective states and controlled operations and entanglement capture coexisting, ambivalent appraisals; the framework covers feature encoding, relevance and valence appraisal, use intentions and the trade-off between involvement and distance. The paper presents the full circuitry of the framework and argues that it relates quantum algorithms to (neuro)psychological processes. The paper reports no empirical validation: no human data, no run on a robot, and no comparison with the original fuzzy system or a classical probabilistic model, and whether circuits were executed on a simulator or hardware is not clear. The contribution is therefore a formal design showing how an existing affective architecture for social robots could be mapped onto gate-based quantum computation. It is relevant to the survey as the most complete quantum rendering of an established robot-affect model.

Summary: Chella et al. (2022) formulate robot motion planning as a production system whose rule application in the recognise–act cycle is carried out by a quantum search. A mobile robot on a grid (taxicab) map with obstacles must find a sequence of moves to a goal; the move rules and a goal test are compiled from Boolean logic into reversible quantum circuits and embedded as the oracle of Grover's algorithm, so that all move sequences of a given length are searched in superposition. The authors work through a 2×2 map and a 4×4 map and propose circuit-level techniques, such as uncomputing to reuse qubits and adding trivial solutions to keep the solution ratio favourable. Because the full 4×4 circuit would need 54 qubits, they simulate a pruned 20-qubit instance with one Grover iteration in Qiskit Aer on a laptop; the two correct two-move paths receive clearly amplified probabilities. They argue analytically that the speed-up holds when the average branching factor exceeds the square root of the maximum branching factor, which their maps satisfy. Limitations are the tiny maps, noiseless simulation, a known static environment, and no comparison with classical planners in runtime. For robotics it is a concrete demonstration of what gate-based quantum planning currently costs in qubits.

Summary: Song et al. (2022) apply quantum cognition to a core autonomous-driving problem: estimating the intentions of pedestrians whose behaviour may be boundedly rational. They argue that classical models assume fully rational traffic participants, whereas real crossing decisions often violate classical probability. Using a quantum-like Bayesian (QLB) network, in which probabilities are obtained from complex amplitudes and interference terms modify the classical law of total probability, they model pedestrian crossing decisions. A case analysis is used to argue that the QLB model captures apparently unreasonable crossing behaviour better than a classical probability model, and a trajectory-prediction experiment on pedestrian trajectory data compares the QLB-based predictor with the data-driven Social-LSTM, reporting that QLB covers edge events in interactive scenes and is closer to real trajectories. All computation is quantum-like, on classical hardware. The exact datasets and error figures could not be verified here, and the interference parameters appear to be set rather than learned, which limits claims of generality; the scenarios are also limited to pedestrian crossing. The paper is one of the few applications of quantum-like Bayesian networks (cf. Moreira and Wichert (2016)) to a safety-critical perception-and-prediction problem for autonomous vehicles.

Summary: Widdows et al. (2023) show that some established quantum-probability models of human judgement can be written as small quantum circuits and executed on real quantum hardware. They build circuit components for question-order effects (non-commuting projections, illustrated with the Clinton–Gore poll, following question-order models such as Wang et al. (2014)), for 'subjective bias' via entanglement with an extra qubit, and for interference in disjunction effects, combining them into a circuit that reproduces the Prisoner's Dilemma pattern and, with other parameters, the two-stage gamble and Hawaii vacation problems of Shafir and Tversky (1992). All circuits use four qubits or fewer and were run with 10,000 shots on an 11-qubit IonQ trapped-ion machine. The Prisoner's Dilemma circuits reproduced the target defection probabilities (82%, 73% and 64% for partner betrays, cooperates or unknown) with a largest discrepancy of 0.37%, while order-effect circuits were within about 2–3% of expected values, comparable to the reported two-qubit gate fidelity. The authors stress that this is not a quantum advantage and not a claim that brains use qubits; parameters are set by hand from published effects rather than fitted to new data. For agent design, it offers reusable circuit 'components' for embedding quantum-like decision biases directly on quantum hardware.

Summary: Mannone et al. (2024) adopt the D'Ariano–Faggin view, in which thinking and consciousness are described by quantum-state dynamics and mental complexity by entanglement of 'qualia' states, and use it to model a robot's inner processing as a quantum–classical dialogue. Their case study is improvised robot dance: classical, periodic multisensory stimuli (visual and auditory, each encoded as calm or activating) are fed into a small quantum circuit representing the dancer's inner state, and measurement outcomes are mapped to a repertoire of poses. The authors report that the circuit uses three qubits with controlled-Hadamard and Toffoli gates and is run on the IBM Qiskit simulator; a second case study adds environmental feedback so that repeated cycles produce increasingly unpredictable sequences, which the authors interpret as creativity, and one run shows reduced activity when an excited state is stimulated further, read as sensory overload. The results are preliminary and illustrative: initial states are set by hand, stimuli are binary, and there is no evaluation of the resulting behaviour by observers or comparison with a classical stochastic controller. The paper is relevant as an example of quantum circuits used as a generative 'inner state' for expressive robot behaviour rather than as an optimiser.

Summary: Daglarli (2025) proposes a brain-inspired cognitive architecture for an autonomous game agent that combines a computational prefrontal-cortex model (meta-cognition and situation awareness), a transformer-based deep reinforcement learning module, and quantum algorithms. Deutsch–Jozsa and Bernstein–Vazirani circuits are used during training to classify environmental states and extract bit patterns, and Grover's search is placed in the decision loop to amplify the probability of high-reward actions; all circuits are written in Qiskit and run on a classical simulator. The agent is evaluated in Minecraft (with the MineRL human-play dataset) on 'explorer', 'survivor' and mixed scenarios, comparing configurations with and without the quantum components. The abstract reports that the quantum-enhanced agent reaches an 80% task success rate about twice as fast and obtains roughly 15% higher cumulative reward than a classical deep RL baseline, with smaller gains in highly uncertain, reactive scenarios; much of the results section is qualitative, and details on runs and statistical testing are limited. Because the quantum routines are classically simulated, any 'speed-up' cannot be physical, and the role of Deutsch–Jozsa and Bernstein–Vazirani in learning is weakly motivated. The paper illustrates how quantum algorithms are being embedded in agent architectures, but its evidence should be read cautiously.

Summary: De Carolis et al. (2025) present a short state-of-the-art review that forms the first task of QUADRI, an Italian project on quantum-enhanced human–robot interaction. Drawing on more than 35 papers published between 2021 and 2025, they group work into reviews and theoretical foundations, quantum-based cognitive models for robots (including Ho and Hoorn (2022), Mannone et al. (2024) and Widdows et al. (2023)), quantum and quantum-inspired emotion recognition and decision-making, and quantum approaches to path finding and navigation (including Hohenfeld et al. (2024)). The project aims to connect a social robot to a quantum simulator and to replace some reinforcement-learning and agent-based components with quantum search (e.g. Grover) and quantum machine learning, focusing on verbal interaction. The authors conclude that hardware limits on qubit numbers are the main common obstacle and that hybrid designs, perceiving the environment classically and processing selected information quantumly, are preferable for now. The paper offers no implementation or evaluation, mixes genuinely quantum, quantum-like and quantum-inspired methods without distinguishing them, and repeats some favourable claims uncritically. It is useful as a map of current social-robotics interest in quantum methods.

Summary: Chella et al. (2026) propose a hybrid classical–quantum architecture for a teleo-reactive robot, i.e. an agent that must classify its perceived situation and select an action under uncertainty arising from sensor noise, ambiguous perceptual configurations or poorly separable action regions. A classical sensor vector is mapped into a quantum feature space in which learned concepts or rule-defined perceptual regions are stored as reference states, and similarities between the current perception and these references support action selection. Two implementations are evaluated offline on a public wall-following robot dataset: a quantum-kernel classifier using ZZ feature maps with a support-vector classifier, compared with a classical RBF kernel, and an illustrative circuit that encodes sensor conditions directly into qubits and selects actions by measurement after amplitude amplification. The authors report that configurations with two sensors performed better than four, and the circuit reached an accuracy of about 0.91 on the two-sensor test set, with errors concentrated near boundaries between action regions. The authors state explicitly that this is an offline proxy for reactive control, not a closed-loop controller and not evidence of quantum advantage. The paper extends the group's earlier quantum planner (Chella et al. (2022)) from deliberative planning to reactive perception–action mapping.

Summary: Eisert et al. (1999) introduced a quantisation scheme for two-player games in which players' strategies act as local unitary operations on an entangled pair of qubits. Applied to the Prisoner's Dilemma, the scheme removes the dilemma when players may use quantum strategies. This review cites it as the origin of quantum game theory, on which later quantum game models of multi-agent interaction, such as automated-driving decisions, build.

Summary: Martinez-Martinez and Sanchez-Burillo (2016) model a decision-maker as an open quantum system whose choice probabilities arise as the stationary distribution of a quantum stochastic walk (QSW) on a 'cognitive network'. The network extends a classical decision tree: nodes are action–state combinations, connected components correspond to states of the world, and edge weights combine a profitability matrix built from Luce's choice axiom (with a discrimination parameter) and a belief-formation matrix. Dynamics follow a Lindblad–Kossakowski master equation, and a single parameter interpolates between purely unitary (quantum walk) and purely dissipative (classical random walk) evolution; uniqueness of the stationary state is proved via Spohn's theorem. A Prisoner's Dilemma case study shows that the model can reproduce violations of the sure-thing principle and of the law of total probability. The work is formal and illustrative, not fitted to new behavioural data, and it adds free parameters. For autonomous agents it offers a concrete open-system (Lindblad) decision mechanism that converges to a well-defined choice distribution, a template for agents that must settle on actions over time.

Summary: Yukalov et al. (2018) extend quantum decision theory (QDT; cf. Yukalov and Sornette (2011)) from single individuals to a society of interacting decision-makers taking decisions in multistep processes. Each agent evaluates prospects by two criteria: a utility factor (rational, classical part) and an attraction factor (quantum interference term reflecting subconscious attractiveness). Agents exchange information between steps, and this exchange progressively reduces the attraction (interference) term. The model yields three predictions about the dynamic disjunction effect: behaviour is initially probabilistic and deviates from utility-based choice; as information accumulates, prospect probabilities converge towards the utility factors; and repeated information sharing leads to a consensus. The authors report that these predictions agree closely with empirical observations on the dynamic disjunction effect, although the comparison relies on existing experimental results rather than a new study. The framework is quantum-like, being operator-based QP on classical computation, and its agent-interaction rules are stylised. For multi-agent AI, it gives an analytically tractable account of how communication between agents can damp irrational (interference-driven) choice and produce collective convergence.

Summary: Ried et al. (2019) propose modelling collective motion with learning agents rather than featureless self-propelled particles with pre-specified interaction rules. Each individual is a projective simulation (PS) agent (Briegel and De las Cuevas (2012)): percepts and actions are 'clips' in an episodic memory network, decisions are random walks over the network, and edge weights (h-values) are reinforced by reward with a forgetting (damping) term. In the marching-locust case study, agents in a one-dimensional ring world (80 cells, sensory range 5) perceive the net flow of nearby conspecifics, may either continue or turn around, and are rewarded for moving with the local majority. With N = 10, 40 and 70 agents the learned behaviour reproduces the known density-dependent regimes: disordered motion, alignment with periodic switching, and stable long-term alignment; individual response probabilities converge within roughly 10² time-steps, and a Fokker–Planck analysis gives drift and diffusion coefficients that qualitatively match experimental locust data. PS here is a classical reinforcement-learning model whose design is inspired by quantum-walk ideas; no quantum hardware or QP is used. The setting is minimal (1-D, two actions). For robot swarms, it shows how interaction rules can emerge from individual reward rather than being hand-coded.

Summary: Khoshnoud et al. (2020) explore whether experimental quantum-optical resources can be embedded in cooperative multi-robot systems. The work is genuinely hardware-based rather than quantum-like: photonic components (laser diode, half-wave plates, polarising beam splitter, single-photon counters, and a spontaneous parametric down-conversion source with a BBO crystal producing 810 nm polarisation-entangled pairs) are mounted on classical mobile platforms (Arlo ground robots and a DJI Mavic 2 drone), with Pixy2 cameras and servo motors keeping the optical path aligned. Two demonstrations are described. In the first, a BB84-style polarisation protocol between an 'Alice' and a 'Bob' robot yields binary outcomes that are mapped directly to motion commands on the onboard microcontrollers, with an eavesdropper robot illustrating intrusion detection. In the second, coincidence detection of entangled photon pairs on two robots triggers identical actions under a leader robot. The paper is largely a tutorial and concept demonstration: it reports no quantitative performance data (key rates, error rates, alignment accuracy or latency), and some demonstrations use attenuated laser pulses rather than true single photons. Claims of 'very fast' entanglement-based coordination should be read against the no-signalling theorem, which the paper does not discuss. For autonomous agents, it remains one of the few physical demonstrations of quantum communication hardware on moving robots, useful as a contrast to quantum-like cognitive models.

Summary: Lopez-Incera et al. (2020) use projective simulation (PS; Briegel and De las Cuevas (2012)), a transparent reinforcement-learning model with episodic and compositional memory, to study how swarm behaviour develops under different foraging pressures. Each of 60 agents in a one-dimensional circular world (500 positions) perceives neighbour density and orientation within a visual range of six positions (25 percepts), chooses to continue or turn around, and is rewarded for reaching a food source placed at varying distance. Training runs for 10,000 trials per scenario. When food is distant (e.g. 21 positions), strongly aligned swarms emerge (alignment order parameter around 0.8 or higher) after roughly 200 trials; when food is near, agents remain weakly aligned (about 0.2). Individual trajectories differ accordingly: distant-resource agents show composite correlated random walks resembling Lévy walks, whereas nearby-resource agents show mainly Brownian motion. As in Ried et al. (2019), PS is a classical algorithm with quantum-walk motivation; quantum speed-ups are not exercised. Limitations are the 1-D world, binary actions and a single reward type. For robotics, it shows that collective strategies suited to the task (search versus exploitation) can be learned rather than prescribed, with an interpretable policy.

Summary: Lawless (2020) argues that no adequate mathematics yet exists for designing and safely operating autonomous human–machine teams (A-HMTs), and that rational, individual-level models fail under the uncertainty in which such teams operate. He proposes interdependence theory with quantum-like properties: bistability (an analogue of wave–particle duality, e.g. two competing interpretations of reality), a measurement problem (measuring one aspect of a team increases uncertainty about its complement) and non-factorability (team performance cannot be decomposed into individual contributions, an analogue of entanglement and the no-cloning theorem). The argument draws on entropy production and Kullback–Leibler divergence and is contrasted with six field case studies, including the USS Greeneville and USS McCain collisions, the USS Vincennes incident and the Uber autonomous-vehicle fatality. A central claim is that a machine teammate must be able to explain itself to humans in causal language. The paper is conceptual; the quantum analogies are not formalised as a fitted QP model, and the case studies are interpreted qualitatively. For autonomous systems it frames why team-level, context-dependent models, rather than aggregation of individual models, may be needed for trustworthy human–machine teaming.

Summary: Waddup et al. (2021) define sensitivity to context for two agents each answering two binary questions: responses to one agent's question depend on which question the other agent faces, so that the joint probabilities cannot be represented by a single four-way distribution. They report two experiments with a Prisoner's-Dilemma-like task constructed without a Nash equilibrium; Experiment 1 recruited 100 participants. Behaviour showed sensitivity to context, adding to evidence that such games can be built so that choices are inconsistent with baseline classical probability and with decisions revealing pre-existing values. Two closely matched models, one classical and one quantum, were fitted, and the quantum model fitted better; in it, context sensitivity coincides with (epiphenomenal) entanglement. The effect is shown in one task family, and the classical comparison model is a baseline rather than an exhaustive alternative. For multi-agent AI and human–robot interaction, the result indicates that a partner's choice may depend on the joint question context, which matters when agents predict human responses in interactive settings.

Summary: Yan et al. (2021) propose a quantum affective computing (QAC) framework in which a robot's emotion is a single-qubit state |E(ξ)⟩ = cos ξ|0⟩ + sin ξ|1⟩, with the angle ξ placing the emotion on a bipolar spectrum. Standard gates acquire affective readings: X inverts an emotion, Z negates its angle, H 'neutralises' it, and Ry rotations increase or decrease emotional intensity; measurement statistics recover the emotion as a probability distribution. For groups, the authors adopt an image-style encoding (akin to flexible quantum image representations) in which robots on a 2ⁿ × 2ⁿ lattice are indexed by 2n position qubits entangled with one emotion qubit, so that 2n + 1 qubits hold the fused emotion of all robots, and controlled rotations change the emotions of chosen sub-regions in one operation. The demonstrations are small classical simulations, for example 64 robots on an 8 × 8 lattice split into quadrants, showing probability distributions before and after controlled rotations. The paper itself notes that state preparation costs O(2⁴ⁿ) elementary operations and that read-out requires many repeated measurements, which offsets the claimed qubit economy; no hardware runs, human data or behavioural validation are reported. This is a quantum-circuit formalism rather than a quantum-like cognitive model. For multi-robot systems it is a representative example of mapping affective state onto circuits, useful mainly as a design sketch.

Summary: Yun et al. (2022) extend variational quantum circuit (VQC) reinforcement learning to the multi-agent setting. Naively concatenating all agents' state–action pairs would require qubit counts that grow with the number of agents, and hence more noise on NISQ devices; the authors therefore adopt centralised training with decentralised execution (CTDE), giving each agent a VQC actor (softmax over measured expectation values) and using a single VQC centralised critic whose input is compressed by a rotation-gate state encoder. The method is evaluated in a simulated single-hop edge-to-cloud packet-offloading environment (two clouds, four edge agents, four qubits per actor/critic, 50 variational gates), implemented with torchquantum and PyTorch on a GPU rather than on quantum hardware, citing cloud latency. With 50 trainable parameters for all constrained models, the proposed QMARL reached a total reward of about −3.0 (90.9% 'achievability' after min–max normalisation) against −16.6 for a hybrid VQC-actor/classical-critic variant and −22.5 for a parameter-matched classical CTDE baseline; the headline claim is a 57.7% reward improvement. However, a classical baseline with more than 40K parameters scored −2.8 (91.5%), so the advantage holds only under an equal-parameter constraint. The study is a single, small, noiseless simulation without statistical repeats. For autonomous agents, it illustrates quantum-circuit (not quantum-like) policies and their current evidential limits.

Summary: Yukalov et al. (2022) study networks of agents operating under quantum decision theory, in which each agent evaluates alternatives by utility, attractiveness and the information available to it, so that choice is a multimodal process. Information reaches agents in two forms: direct agent-to-agent exchange and a collective information field generated by the whole society. For agents with short-term memory, decision probabilities often oscillate for a prolonged period before settling. Adding the collective information field smooths sharp variations in temporal behaviour, reduces oscillation amplitude, can remove oscillations entirely and forces convergence to fixed limits; the model also reproduces the dynamic disjunction effect. The work builds on Yukalov et al. (2018) and is analytical and numerical; no new behavioural data are collected and the communication structure is idealised. The formalism is quantum-like (QP maths on classical computation). For multi-agent AI, it suggests that a shared broadcast signal, such as a common operating picture, can stabilise otherwise oscillating collective decisions.
